# github.com/coredhcp/coredhcp/plugins/sleep

Package sleep holds the plugin chain still for a fixed duration, so that a slow server can be produced on purpose. It is a test aid, for both families: client timeouts, retransmission behaviour and the server's own in-flight limit all need a handler that takes its time, and nothing else in the tree provides one.

	server4:
	  plugins:
	    - sleep: 300ms
	    - file: leases4.txt

	server6:
	  plugins:
	    - sleep: 1s
	    - file: leases6.txt

The only argument is the delay, and it is required. It is written the Go way, as time.ParseDuration reads it: 300ms, 1s, 2m30s. Anything other than exactly one argument fails setup, and so does a value ParseDuration rejects, both with the argument quoted. A negative duration parses and then sleeps for no time at all, because time.Sleep returns straight away for anything at or below zero.

## Not in the shipped binary

sleep is deliberately absent from cmd/coredhcp and from the plugin list the generator reads, cmd/coredhcp-generator/core-plugins.txt, so the server built by \`make build\` does not have it and a configuration naming it is refused as an unknown plugin. Build a server that does have it:

	coredhcp-generator --from cmd/coredhcp-generator/core-plugins.txt sleep

## Placement

Anywhere. The plugin never ends the chain and never touches the response, so what it delays is every plugin after it plus the reply itself. Put it directly before whatever is being timed.

## What the delay costs

The sleep happens on the goroutine handling that one packet, which holds one of the server's in-flight slots for the duration. The default limit is eight slots per GOMAXPROCS (see server.WithMaxInFlight), and datagrams arriving with every slot taken are dropped before the chain, counted, and logged as the in-flight handler limit being reached. A delay of any size therefore turns into dropped requests once the arrival rate passes the slot count divided by the delay, which is the property that makes this useful for testing and useless in production.

A client that gives up before the delay is over has already retransmitted, so a delay longer than the client's own timeout produces duplicate requests rather than slow replies.
